intro: Two teams of six skate at high speed, using sticks to shoot a hard rubber puck into the opponents' net. Players change on the fly every minute or so, body checking is part of the men's game, and penalties send players to the box, giving the other team a power play. The IIHF governs international hockey; the NHL has its own rulebook.
inThirtySeconds: Score by getting the puck completely over the goal line into the net.
Offside: attackers can't enter the attacking zone ahead of the puck.
Icing: shooting the puck from your half all the way past the opponents' goal line, untouched, brings a face-off back in your zone.
Penalties put players in the box for 2 or 5 minutes; their team plays short-handed.
objective: Score more goals than the opponent in three 20-minute periods.

facts.players: 6 per team on ice (5 skaters + goaltender), with frequent line changes
facts.environment: Indoor ice rink surrounded by boards and glass

scoring.label: Goal
scoring.detail: The whole puck crosses the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar.

scoring.label: Shootout goal
scoring.detail: In some competitions, a shootout decides tied games; the winner gets one extra goal on the final score.

variants.name: IIHF
variants.description: International rules for World Championships and the Olympics.

variants.name: NHL
variants.description: The National Hockey League's own rulebook, with its own overtime and rink specifications.

bodies.name: International Ice Hockey Federation
bodies.scope: World governing body; publishes the IIHF Official Rule Book

chapters.title: Offside and icing
chapters.summary: The two rules that shape every rush.

rules.title: Offside
rules.summary: An attacking player is offside if both skates are completely over the opponents' blue line before the puck crosses it.
rules.body: The position of the skates, not the stick, matters. Play stops for a face-off outside the zone. Under delayed offside, the attackers can 'tag up' by all leaving the zone before play is stopped.
rules.example: A forward glides across the blue line a stride before his teammate carries the puck in: offside, face-off in the neutral zone.

rules.title: Icing
rules.summary: If a team shoots the puck from its own side of the centre red line all the way across the opponents' goal line, untouched, it is icing.
rules.body: Play restarts with a face-off in the offending team's defensive zone, and the team that iced the puck cannot change players. A short-handed team (killing a penalty) is allowed to ice the puck. Both the IIHF and NHL use hybrid icing, where the linesman judges a race for the puck to decide whether to call it.

chapters.title: Penalties
chapters.summary: The penalty box and power plays.

rules.title: Minor penalties
rules.summary: Infractions such as tripping, hooking, slashing, holding and high-sticking usually cost 2 minutes in the penalty box.
rules.body: The opponents play with an extra skater — a power play. If they score during a minor penalty, the penalised player may return immediately. A double minor (4 minutes) is often given for high-sticking that draws blood.

rules.title: Major penalties and misconducts
rules.summary: Serious infractions — such as fighting or injurious hits — bring 5-minute majors, served in full even if goals are scored.
rules.body: Misconduct penalties (10 minutes) remove a player but not a skater from the ice; game misconducts and match penalties eject the player.

rules.title: Body checking
rules.summary: In men's hockey, using the hip or shoulder to check an opponent who has the puck is legal; checks to the head, from behind or into the boards dangerously are not.
rules.body: Body checking is prohibited in women's hockey under IIHF rules and in many youth levels.

chapters.title: Goals and overtime
chapters.summary: What counts and how ties are broken.

rules.title: Disallowed goals
rules.summary: A goal is disallowed if the puck is deliberately kicked in, batted in with a high stick, or if an attacker interferes with the goaltender.
rules.body: Video review is used for close calls on whether the puck crossed the line, and coaches can challenge for offside or goaltender interference.

rules.title: NHL overtime
rules.summary: Tied regular-season games go to 5 minutes of 3-on-3 sudden-death overtime, then a shootout.
rules.body: In the playoffs, overtime is 5-on-5 with full 20-minute periods until someone scores.

rules.title: IIHF overtime
rules.summary: Tied games go to sudden-death overtime, and in many stages a game-winning shot shootout.
rules.body: The length and format of overtime depend on the tournament stage; medal games use longer overtime periods.

fouls.name: Tripping / hooking / slashing
fouls.description: Using the stick to impede an opponent.

fouls.name: High-sticking
fouls.description: Contacting an opponent with the stick above the shoulders.

flow.title: Opening face-off
flow.description: The referee drops the puck at centre ice.

flow.title: Shifts
flow.description: Lines change every 40–60 seconds, often on the fly.

flow.title: Intermissions
flow.description: Breaks between periods; teams change ends.

flow.title: Empty net
flow.description: Late in games, trailing teams pull the goaltender for an extra attacker.

positions.name: Centre
positions.role: Takes face-offs and links defence and attack.

positions.name: Wingers
positions.role: Left and right wings, mainly attackers.

positions.name: Defencemen
positions.role: Two players protecting their zone and starting rushes.

field.name: Rink
field.dimensions: NHL: 200 ft × 85 ft (about 61 × 26 m); IIHF rinks may be wider
field.surface: Ice, enclosed by boards and glass
notes: Red centre line and two blue lines
